section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Binary Language
section_1.content: Introduce binary as a base-2 system. Explain that just as decimal uses 10 digits (0-9), binary uses only 0 and 1, where each position represents a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8...).
section_1.example: Visual: A row of 4 light bulbs. Each bulb represents a bit. Bulb ON = 1, Bulb OFF = 0. Show how 1011 in binary equals 8+0+2+1 = 11 in decimal.

section_2.title: The Towers of Hanoi Puzzle
section_2.content: Define the classic puzzle: 3 rods and n discs of different sizes. Rules: Move one disc at a time, never place a larger disc on a smaller one. The goal is to move the full stack to a target rod.
section_2.example: Visual: 3 discs on Peg A. Animation shows the sequence of moves required to shift the stack to Peg C, emphasizing the recursive nature of the puzzle.

section_3.title: Mapping Moves to Binary Codes
section_3.content: Explain the surprising link: If we number the moves from 1 to 2^n - 1, the disc to be moved corresponds to the position of the lowest set bit in the binary representation of the move number.
section_3.example: Visual: A table comparing Move Number (1-7), its Binary form (001, 010, 011...), and the disc to move (Disc 1, 2, 1, 3...). Use a character, 'Robo-Solver', pointing at the specific disc for each step.

section_4.title: The Binary Direction Rule
section_4.content: Define the direction of the moves based on binary state. For odd discs, moves go in a specific cycle; for even discs, the opposite cycle.
section_4.example: Visual: 'Disk-o-Bot' moves Disc 1 (the smallest) clockwise among pegs, while larger discs follow a fixed parity rule based on their binary index, ensuring the puzzle is solved automatically.

section_5.title: Summary and Real-world Application
section_5.content: Synthesize the concept: The puzzle is a physical manifestation of a binary counter. This logic is fundamental to recursive programming and algorithm complexity analysis.
section_5.example: Visual: A final graphic showing a computer processor's clock cycle (0s and 1s) evolving into the movement of Hanoi discs, demonstrating how counting sequences drive mechanical movement.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.0 + j * 1.2
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.9
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: The Binary Language", [
            "Binary systems use only two digits: zero and one.",
            "Each position represents an increasing power of two.",
            "Four bits can represent numbers from zero to fifteen.",
            "Binary is the language of all modern computers."
        ])
        
        # Elements
        bits = Text("001", font_size=48, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(bits, 'C3')
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE), Write(bits))

import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines if not line.startswith("[Asset:")]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT, buff=0.3).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                # Shift right-side grid to the right half
                x = 3.0 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.2 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
